evidence_set: Drug and placebo adverse-event rates were highly correlated (r = 0.89, p < 0.0001) and observed relative risks were close to those predicted from the placebo rate alone; citing Wernicke et al., the authors note that eliciting adverse events gives higher absolute rates in both groups, while spontaneous reporting more often gives larger relative risks; so relative risks should be read with absolute risks, which the review does not report in its text.

evidence_set: MDMA against placebo (2-factor analysis over treatment and recovery nights, df 1 and 6), treatment-night values: total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes, F = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, F = 7.0, P = 0.038; stage 1 8.4 against 6.6%, F = 9.49, P = 0.022; REM 3.5 (2.1) against 19.2 (2.0)%, F = 14.28, P = 0.009, reduced on the treatment night only (interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003); no effect on wake after persistent sleep, stage 2 (P = 0.267), stage 3/4 (P = 0.119) or REM latency (P = 0.589).

Recovery night with placebo after the MDMA session: total sleep 403.6 (SEM 34.4) minutes and REM 22.2% (1.5), against 431.9 minutes and 20.6% on the recovery night of the placebo session; no main effects of night and no night-by-drug interactions except for REM percentage, reduced on the treatment night only.

Only 7 completed; two withdrew and the 12-sequence Latin square was incomplete; the laboratory schedule was earlier than the participants' usual sleep times, which the authors judged unlikely to affect the MDMA-placebo comparison. The abstract states that MDMA reduced stage 3/4 sleep, which the drug comparison does not show (P = 0.119).

evidence_set: Treatment by day interaction F = 4.63 (df 2 and 12), P = 0.032; after shortened sleep the mean nap-test latency was shorter than after placebo (about 6 minutes, per the Discussion), while after MDMA it differed neither from placebo nor from shortened sleep, per the Results text; the Figure 4 legend instead reports shortened sleep as shorter than both placebo and MDMA (P = 0.031), and in the figure the MDMA bar is close to placebo; no differences on the day after the recovery night; sleep-onset REM periods 2.14 (shortened sleep), 1.43 (MDMA), 1.00 (placebo), not significant.

The authors conclude that MDMA's sleep loss was not associated with next-day sleepiness and that next-day sleep latency remained at placebo levels; with 7 participants, MDMA's next-day values were not significantly different from those after shortened sleep either, per the Results text (the Figure 4 legend reports the opposite).
